explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. David says it the other way around: “God arises. His enemies are scattered, and those who hate Him flee His presence.” Nobody in that verse is standing their ground. They're all heading for the exit.

That's it, friend. David says, “…His enemies are scattered, and those who hate Him flee His presence.” When God arises, the ones who hate Him are the ones running. I bet not one of them stops to look back.

You got it, baker. David says, “But the righteous will be glad and rejoice before God; they will celebrate with joy.” The wicked melt like wax, but the righteous are glad to be right there in His presence. Same moment, two very different reactions.

Close, friend, but David has a louder crowd in mind. He says the righteous “will be glad and rejoice before God.” Silence isn't in the verse at all. This is a party, and he says they celebrate with joy.

I get why you'd pick that one, friend. But the trembling and fleeing belong to His enemies in verses 1 and 2. For the righteous, David says they “will be glad and rejoice before God.” They don't hide from His presence. They celebrate in it.

Right, friend. David calls God “Him who rides on the clouds” in verse 4, and then says, “A father of the fatherless and a defender of widows is God in His holy habitation.” It's the same song and the same God. The One up in the clouds is the One who defends widows.

Nope, friend, this one is true. Right after David talks about the One who rides on the clouds, he says, “A father of the fatherless and a defender of widows is God in His holy habitation.” Verse 5 comes right after verse 4. Same song, same God.
Baked right, baker! David says, “God settles the lonely in families…” The lonely don't get left on their own. God puts them in a family. I think that's one of the warmest lines in the whole psalm.
Long lives sound nice, friend, but that's not what David says here. He says, “God settles the lonely in families…” The answer is about who surrounds them, not how many years they get.
That would be a big jump from lonely to ruling, friend. But David doesn't say it. He says, “God settles the lonely in families…” For someone who's been on their own, I think a family is plenty.

That's it, friend. David says, “the earth shook and the heavens poured down rain before God, the One on Sinai…” (Psalm 68:8). When God marched, the ground itself felt it. Even the earth had a reaction.

I like the calm of that one, friend, but it's not in the verse. David says, “the earth shook and the heavens poured down rain before God…” (Psalm 68:8). Nothing rests when God marches through the wasteland. The earth shakes.

That's a dramatic guess, friend, and it fits the mood. But David's word is shook: “the earth shook and the heavens poured down rain before God…” (Psalm 68:8). Rain came down from above, and the ground trembled below.

You got it, baker. David says, “You sent abundant rain, O God; You refreshed Your weary inheritance.” His people were weary, and the rain refreshed them. It's like getting a cold glass of water after a long day on your feet.
I see why you'd think that, friend, but testing isn't in the verse. David says, “You sent abundant rain, O God; You refreshed Your weary inheritance.” For people who were weary, the rain was a gift.
Abundant rain can sound like a flood, friend, and I'll admit I'd check the roof. But David doesn't say flooded. He says, “You refreshed Your weary inheritance.” That rain was a refreshing one.
Right on, baker! David says, “O God, from Your bounty You provided for the poor.” The bounty is God's, and the poor are who He provides for. That's a good thing to be able to say about someone.
Nice try, friend, but kings aren't named in this verse. David says, “O God, from Your bounty You provided for the poor.” The ones who get provided for are the poor.
Priests are a fair guess, friend, but David doesn't mention them here. He says, “O God, from Your bounty You provided for the poor.” God's bounty goes to the poor.
That's it, baker. The women's song says, “Kings and their armies flee in haste…” (Psalm 68:12). It's a whole army, and they aren't marching anywhere but away. Haste means they're in a big hurry.
That sounds nice and orderly, friend, but it's not what the women sing. They say, “Kings and their armies flee in haste…” (Psalm 68:12). Nobody in that line calmly puts down a sword. They run.
I can see it, friend, kings and armies on the move. But the women sing that they “flee in haste.” (Psalm 68:12) They're running from the battle, not toward it.

You got it, baker. The song says, “…she who waits at home divides the plunder.” The one who stayed home is the one dividing it up. It's like the person who skipped the long meeting and still gets the good news first.
Guards at the gate is a fair thought, friend, but the song never mentions them. It says, “…she who waits at home divides the plunder.” The one dividing the plunder is the one waiting at home.
You'd expect the captains to take the prize, friend. But the song doesn't say that. The armies are the ones who flee, and “she who waits at home divides the plunder.”

explanations.answer: The mountain God chose to dwell on
explanations.explanation: Perfect, baker. David asks, “Why do you gaze in envy, O mountains of many peaks?” and answers, “This is the mountain God chose for His dwelling…” Those big mountains with all their peaks are looking at the one God chose. I think that's a lot of mountain jealousy.
Armies make sense for a psalm like this, friend, but David doesn't put them here. The mountains gaze at “the mountain God chose for His dwelling…” That's what they envy.
Rivers are a pretty picture, friend, but they aren't in this verse. David says the mountains are looking at “the mountain God chose for His dwelling…” That's the mountain they envy.
Right, baker. David says of the chosen mountain, “…where the LORD will surely dwell forever.” Surely and forever, both in one line. That's about as settled as it gets.
This one is true, friend. David says of the mountain God chose, “…where the LORD will surely dwell forever.” He doesn't say for a while. He says forever.

Not even close, friend. David says the chariots of God are tens of thousands, thousands of thousands. Hundreds would be a rounding error next to that. And he says the Lord is in His sanctuary as He was at Sinai.
That's it, baker. David doesn't say hundreds. He says the chariots of God are tens of thousands, thousands of thousands. That's way past what I could count, even with a helper.

explanations.answer: So the LORD God may dwell there
explanations.explanation: Baked right, baker! David says God received gifts, even from the rebellious, “…that the LORD God may dwell there.” The ascending, the captives and the gifts all lead to God dwelling there. David gives that as the reason.

explanations.answer: So the nations will fear Israel
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, friend, but David never says it. He says God received gifts “…that the LORD God may dwell there.” The point is God dwelling there, not anyone fearing Israel.

explanations.answer: So the priests will have plenty
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so, friend, but priests aren't in the verse. David says God received gifts, even from the rebellious, “…that the LORD God may dwell there.” That's the reason he gives.
You got it, baker. David says, “Our God is a God of deliverance; the Lord GOD is our rescuer from death.” Not just from trouble. From death itself. That's about as far as rescue can reach.
Sickness is a real thing to be rescued from, friend, but it isn't the word David uses. He says, “the Lord GOD is our rescuer from death.” The rescue goes all the way to death.
That's a heavy thing to carry, friend, but David doesn't name shame here. He says, “the Lord GOD is our rescuer from death.” That's how far he says the rescue reaches.

I think this one is a heavy verse, friend. David says the opposite of making peace: “Surely God will crush the heads of His enemies, the hairy crowns of those who persist in guilty ways.” The ones who keep going in guilty ways are the ones he says God will crush.

That's it, baker. I think this verse is heavy. David says, “Surely God will crush the heads of His enemies, the hairy crowns of those who persist in guilty ways.” He doesn't say God makes peace with them.

You got it, baker. David says, “The singers lead the way, the musicians follow after, among the maidens playing tambourines.” The singers are out in front and the musicians come right behind them. Not a quiet group, I'd say.
Soldiers would look impressive, friend, but David doesn't put them here. He says, “The singers lead the way, the musicians follow after…” In this parade, the singers go first.
Elders are a fair guess for a parade like this, friend, but David doesn't mention them. He says, “The singers lead the way, the musicians follow after…” The ones up front are the singers.

Right, baker. David says, “Bless God in the great congregation; bless the LORD from the fountain of Israel.” He's calling for a big crowd to bless God together. It's a call for everybody, not for a quiet corner.
This one is true, friend. After the procession, David says, “Bless God in the great congregation; bless the LORD from the fountain of Israel.” That's right in verse 26.

Baked right, baker! David says, “Because of Your temple at Jerusalem kings will bring You gifts.” Kings are coming, and they come carrying gifts for God. It's a good thing to show up with something in your hands.
That's a very kingly guess, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. David says, “Because of Your temple at Jerusalem kings will bring You gifts.” The kings bring gifts, not armies.
I can see a king showing up with a warning, friend. But David says, “Because of Your temple at Jerusalem kings will bring You gifts.” These kings come bringing gifts.

explanations.answer: The ones who delight in war
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. David prays, “Scatter the nations who delight in war.” He names them by what they enjoy, and it's war. That's the one he asks God to scatter.

explanations.answer: The ones who live far away
explanations.explanation: Distance sounds like a reasonable thing to pick, friend, but David doesn't use it. He prays, “Scatter the nations who delight in war.” It's about what they delight in, not where they live.

explanations.answer: The ones who trade with Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's a clever guess, friend, but trade isn't in the verse. Envoys arriving from Egypt come up in the very next verse, in a different thought. In verse 30, David prays, “Scatter the nations who delight in war.”

explanations.answer: Stretch out her hands to God
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David says, “Envoys will arrive from Egypt; Cush will stretch out her hands to God.” Egypt sends envoys and Cush reaches out her hands to God. It's a picture of two lands turning toward Him.
Closed gates would be a different song, friend. David says, “Cush will stretch out her hands to God.” Her hands are reaching out, not shutting anything.

explanations.answer: Send her armies to the north
explanations.explanation: Armies come up in this psalm, friend, but not here. David says, “Cush will stretch out her hands to God.” That's what Cush does in this verse.
Not quite, friend. David says God's “majesty is over Israel, whose strength is in the skies.” His strength isn't stuck down on the earth. It's in the skies.

You got it, baker. David says, “Ascribe the power to God, whose majesty is over Israel, whose strength is in the skies.” His majesty is over Israel, and His strength is in the skies. It's up there, not down on the ground.
